items.title: [FDD Diary #19] Manual Testing Hell
content:
Changed the notification text.
Check everything again.
Login. Agent. Notification. Settings.
Thirty minutes.

Another fix. Everything again. Thirty minutes.
Another fix. Everything again. Thirty minutes.

"Do I have to check everything every time I make a change?"

Yes.
Because if you don't, you won't know what broke.

Around the fifth check, things change.

"This has nothing to do with what I just changed."
"This one probably didn't break."

Skip it.
That's exactly the door bugs walk through.

Willpower runs out.
Fifth check -- focus drops.
Tenth -- you start skimming.
Twentieth -- you stop looking.

Manual testing isn't a time problem.
It's a willpower problem.

Fifty features means fifty boxes.

Have to open each one.
Don't want to? "Probably fine." Skip.
Skip and a dead cat stays in the box.

Schrodinger's error.
Can't tell if there's a bug until you run the code.

Gets discovered later.
At the worst possible moment.
Always.

Is there a way out of this loop?

items.title: [FDD Diary #20] Defining Done
content:
Asked the AI.
"I don't want to check everything every time."
"Write tests."

Tests? I can't read code. Tests are code.
How am I supposed to do that?

"A test is writing down 'if this works, it's done.'"

Wait.

Spec: "When a user logs in, the dashboard appears."
That's what you're building.

Test: "Click login. Dashboard appears. Username displayed."
That's how you confirm it's built.

Spec is the destination.
Test is the arrival confirmation.

The key is you write it first.

Not after writing code.
Before.

"Login shows the dashboard."
Write that down first.
Code passes this bar? "Done."
Doesn't pass? "Not done."

No bar means you can't tell "done" from "probably done."

TDD. Test-Driven Development.
Another grand name. Simple essence.
Setting the bar for "done" first.

"But how do I write tests?"

You don't.
You just set the bar.

"Login shows the dashboard."
"Notification fires exactly once."
"Settings change gets saved."

Plain language. Give that to the AI.
"Write test code that matches this bar."
AI writes it.

Decisions are mine.
Implementation is the AI's.
Verification is the test's.

The thing AI can't do is always a decision.

items.title: [FDD Diary #21] 6,260 Safety Nets
content:
Started with five tests. Ran them. Thirty seconds. All passed.

Five became fifty. Fifty became five hundred.
Run five hundred. One minute. All pass.

"If even one out of five hundred fails, something's broken."
One minute. Automatic.

That code I just changed. Did it break anything?
Run tests. Thirty seconds. All PASS.
"Nope."

Hard to describe that moment.
"Safe to change."
That certainty. Never had it before.

Now there are 6,260 tests.
849 in Rust. 5,411 in TypeScript.
Run them all in one minute.

One minute confirms 6,260 features are correct.

"Can I delete this function?"
Run tests. All pass. Yes, delete it.

"Can I restructure this?"
Run tests. Three fail. Fix three. Run again. All pass.
Yes, restructure it.

Without tests, I was too scared to touch anything.
With tests, I cut without hesitation.

Tests aren't feature verification.
They're courage.

All 6,260 passed. Pushed to production.
69 issues showed up in the real world.

Tests aren't perfect.
They only check situations I thought of.
Different browsers. Slow networks. Unexpected click orders.

But when those 69 showed up?
It wasn't panic. It was a list.
Fixed one by one. Added a test each time.
69 became 0. 6,260 became 6,329.

Tests aren't perfect.
But they're 6,260 times better than nothing.
